title: Exploring Electronics
description: Electronics from first principles — voltage, current, resistance, and circuit design explained clearly. Real components, real numbers, no prior knowledge assumed.

items.title: Home
items.content_html: Electronics from first principles — voltage, current, resistance, and circuit design explained clearly. Real components, real numbers, no prior knowledge assumed.

items.title: AC vs DC
items.content_html: Why outlet power reverses 60 times a second, how a generator makes a sine wave, and why a '120 V' outlet actually peaks near 170 V. Frequency, RMS, and waveforms explained.

items.title: Reading an Analog Sensor
items.content_html: Digital pins only know HIGH and LOW. Wire an MCP9700A temperature sensor to an Arduino and use analogRead() to measure a continuous voltage instead.

items.title: Cells and Batteries
items.content_html: How cells and batteries work: EMF, capacity, internal resistance, series and parallel, eight common chemistries compared, and how to charge, store, and dispose of them safely.

items.title: Blink an LED
items.content_html: Wire a single-LED circuit on a breadboard and flash the Blink sketch to an Arduino — your first complete loop from wiring to running code on real hardware.

items.title: Capacitors
items.content_html: How a capacitor stores charge between two plates, what a farad is, why it fills on an RC curve, and how a camera flash turns two AA cells into a 15 kW burst.

items.title: Overview
items.content_html: The fourteen Circuit Foundations articles in reading order: charge, voltage, current, resistance, Ohm's law, AC, magnetism, capacitors, and inductors, with real numbers.

items.title: Overview
items.content_html: The Communication articles in reading order: serial between two devices, the I²C bus for many sensors on two wires, and fast SPI with a wire per device.

items.title: Overview
items.content_html: The Components articles in reading order: resistors, diodes and LEDs, transistors, vacuum tubes, temperature sensors, and the physical packages parts come in.

items.title: Conductors, Insulators, and Semiconductors
items.content_html: Why copper, silver, and gold conduct electricity and glass doesn't, explained from the atom up: free electrons, collisions, heat, and real numbers.

items.title: Current
items.content_html: What an amp actually is: coulombs of charge per second, counted at one point and never used up. Direction, junctions, measuring in series, and why current is what hurts.

items.title: Digital Pins
items.content_html: A digital pin is either on or off — nothing in between. Learn how a microcontroller drives an LED and reads a button, and why each pin needs a resistor.

items.title: Diodes and LEDs
items.content_html: How a diode lets current through one way only, why every LED colour has its own forward voltage, how to size an LED resistor properly, and what diodes do in real circuits.

items.title: I²C
items.content_html: How the I²C bus lets an Arduino talk to many sensors on two wires: open-drain lines and pull-ups, a shared clock, 7-bit addresses, ACK, and reading an MCP9808.

items.title: Inductors
items.content_html: How an inductor stores energy in a magnetic field and resists any change in current: the henry, what sets a coil's inductance, the L/R time constant, and why switching one off bites.

items.title: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
items.content_html: How magnets work, why a current makes a magnetic field and a moving magnet makes a voltage, and how electromagnets, generators, and transformers use both.

items.title: Metric Prefixes and Units
items.content_html: How metric prefixes work in electronics: what milli, micro, nano, pico, kilo, mega, and giga mean, how to convert between them, and how they're printed on real parts.

items.title: Overview
items.content_html: The Microcontrollers articles in reading order: the Arduino board and its code, digital pins, blinking an LED, reading buttons and analog sensors, and staged output.

items.title: Ohm's Law and Power
items.content_html: Ohm's Law in depth: why current follows voltage in a straight line, which parts break the rule, and how power, heat, and power ratings follow from it.

items.title: Open Circuits, Short Circuits, and Fuses
items.content_html: Why current needs a complete loop, what a short circuit really is, and how a fuse protects a circuit: current, voltage, and speed ratings, with real numbers.
